notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Transport is the movement of people and goods from one place to another.
  • It connects:
  • Production centres.
  • Markets.
  • Ports.
  • Cities.
  • Villages.
  • Resource regions.
  • Efficient transport reduces time and cost of movement.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Transport → Movement of People + Goods

2. Importance of Transport

Transport supports:

  • Agriculture.
  • Industry.
  • Trade.
  • Tourism.
  • National integration.
  • Defence.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Regional development.
3. Major Modes of Transport

India uses:

  • Roadways.
  • Railways.
  • Waterways.
  • Airways.
  • Pipelines.
4. Communication — Basic Meaning
  • Communication is the transmission of information from one place or person to another.
  • Modern communication connects people, institutions and markets almost instantly.
5. Major Forms of Communication

Important forms include:

  • Postal services.
  • Telephone.
  • Mobile communication.
  • Radio.
  • Television.
  • Satellite communication.
  • Internet.
  • Optical-fibre networks.
6. Transport and Economic Development
  • Better transport lowers distribution costs.
  • It allows industries to obtain raw materials and reach markets.
  • Regions with poor connectivity may remain economically isolated.
7. Transport and Geography

Transport routes are influenced by:

  • Relief.
  • Climate.
  • Rivers.
  • Soil.
  • Population.
  • Economic activity.
  • Technology.
8. Transport in Plains
  • Plains favour dense transport networks.
  • Roads and railways are easier and cheaper to construct on level terrain.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Northern Plains → Dense Road and Railway Network

9. Transport in Mountains

Mountain transport faces:

  • Steep slopes.
  • Landslides.
  • Snowfall.
  • Deep valleys.
  • High construction costs.

Routes often follow:

  • River valleys.
  • Mountain passes.
  • Tunnels.
10. Transport in Desert Regions

Challenges include:

  • Sand dunes.
  • Sparse population.
  • Extreme temperature.
  • Water scarcity.
11. Transport in Coastal Regions

Coastal areas favour:

  • Ports.
  • Shipping.
  • Fishing harbours.
  • Coastal highways.
  • International trade.
12. Road Transport
  • Roads are the most flexible means of land transport.
  • They provide door-to-door service.
  • Roads are especially useful for:
  • Short distances.
  • Passenger travel.
  • Perishable goods.
13. Advantages of Road Transport

Roadways provide:

  • Flexible routes.
  • Door-to-door delivery.
  • Access to villages.
  • Feeder links to railways and ports.
  • Rapid movement over short and medium distances.
14. Limitations of Road Transport

Road transport may face:

  • Traffic congestion.
  • Higher fuel use.
  • Air pollution.
  • Accident risk.
  • High maintenance costs.
15. Road Density
  • Road density refers to the length of road per unit area.
  • Densely populated plains generally have higher road density than mountains or deserts.
16. Classification of Roads in India

Roads are commonly classified into:

  • National Highways.
  • State Highways.
  • District roads.
  • Rural roads.
  • Urban roads.
  • Expressways.
17. National Highways
  • National Highways connect major:
  • Cities.
  • State capitals.
  • Ports.
  • Industrial centres.
  • Border areas.
  • They form the backbone of long-distance road transport.
18. State Highways
  • State Highways connect important cities and district headquarters within states.
  • They also link state regions with National Highways.
19. District Roads
  • District roads connect:
  • District headquarters.
  • Towns.
  • Villages.
  • Production centres.
20. Rural Roads
  • Rural roads connect villages with:
  • Markets.
  • Schools.
  • Hospitals.
  • Administrative centres.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Rural Roads → Last-Mile Connectivity

21. Expressways
  • Expressways are high-speed, access-controlled roads.
  • Entry and exit are permitted only at designated points.
  • They reduce travel time between major urban and industrial centres.
22. National Highway Numbering
  • National Highways use a systematic numbering pattern.
  • In general:
  • Odd-numbered highways broadly run north-south.
  • Even-numbered highways broadly run east-west.
  • Spur highways may use additional digits.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Odd NH → North-South

Even NH → East-West

23. Golden Quadrilateral
  • Golden Quadrilateral is a major highway network connecting:
  • Delhi.
  • Mumbai.
  • Chennai.
  • Kolkata.
📌Must-Memorise

Golden Quadrilateral → Delhi + Mumbai + Chennai + Kolkata

24. Importance of Golden Quadrilateral

It connects:

  • Major metropolitan cities.
  • Industrial regions.
  • Agricultural markets.
  • Ports.
25. North-South Corridor
  • The North-South Corridor broadly connects northern India with southern India.
  • It improves long-distance movement across the country.
26. East-West Corridor
  • The East-West Corridor broadly connects western India with northeastern/eastern India.
  • It improves cross-country connectivity.
27. Border Roads
  • Border roads are strategically important in frontier regions.
  • They support:
  • Defence movement.
  • Remote settlements.
  • Tourism.
  • Disaster response.
28. Border Roads Organisation
  • Border Roads Organisation is associated with construction and maintenance of strategic roads in difficult border and mountain regions.
📌Must-Memorise

BRO → Strategic Border Roads

29. Mountain Roads

Mountain roads often use:

  • Hairpin bends.
  • Tunnels.
  • Bridges.
  • Retaining walls.
30. Hairpin Bend
  • A hairpin bend is a sharp road turn used to gain or lose elevation on steep slopes.
31. Road Tunnels
  • Tunnels shorten mountain routes.
  • They can avoid:
  • Snow-bound passes.
  • Steep climbs.
  • Landslide-prone sections.
32. Road Transport and Agriculture

Roads help farmers transport:

  • Milk.
  • Vegetables.
  • Fruits.
  • Flowers.
  • Grain.
  • Livestock products.
33. Road Transport and Perishables
  • Road transport is particularly important for perishables because of flexible and direct delivery.
34. Rail Transport — Basic Importance
  • Railways are a major form of long-distance land transport.
  • They are particularly efficient for:
  • Bulk freight.
  • Long-distance passengers.
  • Heavy goods.
35. Advantages of Railways

Railways can move large quantities of:

  • Coal.
  • Iron ore.
  • Cement.
  • Food grains.
  • Petroleum products.

at comparatively lower cost over long distances.

36. Railways and Industrialisation
  • Railway development encouraged:
  • Mining.
  • Steel production.
  • Port trade.
  • Urban growth.
  • Agricultural commercialisation.
37. First Passenger Railway in India
  • India's first passenger railway ran between Bombay, now Mumbai, and Thane.
  • It began operation in 1853.
📌Must-Memorise

First Indian Passenger Train → Mumbai–Thane → 1853

38. Railway Network Distribution

Railways are dense in:

  • Northern Plains.
  • Industrial belts.
  • Major urban corridors.

They are relatively sparse in:

  • Himalayas.
  • Desert areas.
  • Dense forest regions.
  • Some northeastern hill regions.
39. Why Northern Plains Have Dense Railways

Reasons include:

  • Flat terrain.
  • Dense population.
  • Agricultural production.
  • Major cities.
  • Industrial centres.
40. Peninsular Railway Challenges
  • Plateau relief historically required:
  • Cuttings.
  • Tunnels.
  • Bridges.
  • Ghats.
  • Western Ghats are especially challenging.
41. Ghats and Railways

Important Western Ghats railway passages historically include:

  • Bhor Ghat.
  • Thal Ghat.
  • Palghat Gap.
42. Bhor Ghat
  • Bhor Ghat provides an important route through the Western Ghats between the Mumbai-Pune regions.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Bhor Ghat → Mumbai-Pune Route

43. Thal Ghat
  • Thal Ghat is associated with important rail and road routes from Mumbai toward the interior Deccan.
44. Palghat Gap
  • Palghat Gap provides a major natural passage between Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
  • It facilitates:
  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Trade.
📌Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Palghat Gap → Major Kerala–Tamil Nadu Transport Corridor

45. Railway Gauge
  • Railway gauge is the distance between the inner sides of two rails.
  • Different gauges were historically used in India.
46. Broad Gauge
  • Broad gauge is the dominant railway gauge in India.
  • Indian broad gauge measures 1,676 mm.
📌Must-Memorise

Indian Broad Gauge → 1,676 mm

47. Meter Gauge
  • Meter gauge has a width of approximately one metre.
  • Much of India's former meter-gauge network has been converted to broad gauge.
48. Narrow Gauge
  • Narrow-gauge railways have a track width smaller than one metre.
  • Some heritage mountain railways retain narrow gauges.
49. Gauge Conversion
  • Gauge conversion improves:
  • Network integration.
  • Freight movement.
  • Passenger connectivity.
  • It reduces the need for transshipment.
50. Railway Electrification
  • Electrification allows trains to operate using electric traction.
  • Advantages include:
  • Reduced local diesel use.
  • Higher efficiency.
  • Better acceleration.
51. Railway Junction
  • A railway junction is a station where railway lines from different directions meet or diverge.
52. Railway Terminal
  • A terminal is an important starting or ending point for railway services.
53. Freight Corridor — Concept
  • Dedicated freight corridors are rail routes designed primarily for goods transport.
  • Separating freight from passenger traffic can improve capacity and speed.
54. Container Transport
  • Containers allow goods to move efficiently between:
  • Ships.
  • Railways.
  • Trucks.
  • This is called intermodal transport.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Containerisation → Easy Transfer Between Transport Modes

55. Intermodal Transport
  • Intermodal transport uses two or more transport modes without repeatedly handling the cargo itself.
  • Example:
  • Ship → Rail → Truck.
56. Multimodal Transport
  • Multimodal transport combines several modes under coordinated movement.
  • It improves logistics efficiency.
57. Mountain Railways

Important heritage mountain railways include:

  • Darjeeling Himalayan Railway.
  • Nilgiri Mountain Railway.
  • Kalka-Shimla Railway.
58. Darjeeling Himalayan Railway
  • Darjeeling Himalayan Railway lies in West Bengal.
  • It connects the plains with Darjeeling hill region.
59. Nilgiri Mountain Railway
  • Nilgiri Mountain Railway is located in Tamil Nadu.
  • It connects the Mettupalayam region with the Nilgiri highlands.
📌Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Nilgiri Mountain Railway → Mettupalayam–Nilgiris

60. Nilgiri Railway and Rack System
  • Parts of the Nilgiri Mountain Railway use a rack-and-pinion system to climb steep gradients.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Nilgiri Mountain Railway → Rack-and-Pinion

61. Chennai and Indian Railways
  • Chennai is one of southern India's major railway hubs.
  • It connects Tamil Nadu with:
  • Bengaluru.
  • Hyderabad.
  • Mumbai.
  • Delhi.
  • Kolkata.
  • Southern districts.
62. Major Chennai Railway Terminals

Important railway terminals include:

  • Chennai Central.
  • Chennai Egmore.
63. Chennai Central
  • Chennai Central is an important long-distance railway terminal.
  • It connects Chennai with northern, western and other southern regions.
64. Chennai Egmore
  • Chennai Egmore is historically important for rail services toward southern Tamil Nadu.
65. Salem Railway Importance
  • Salem is an important railway junction connecting western, central and southern Tamil Nadu.
66. Erode Railway Importance
  • Erode is a major railway junction in western Tamil Nadu.
  • It lies on important east-west and north-south rail routes.
67. Coimbatore Railway Importance
  • Coimbatore is an important industrial and railway centre of western Tamil Nadu.
  • It connects Tamil Nadu with Kerala through the Palghat Gap.
68. Madurai Railway Importance
  • Madurai is a major railway junction serving southern Tamil Nadu.
69. Tiruchirappalli Railway Importance
  • Tiruchirappalli is one of central Tamil Nadu's major railway junctions.
  • Its central location provides connections in multiple directions.
70. Water Transport — Basic Meaning

Water transport includes:

  • Inland waterways.
  • Coastal shipping.
  • Ocean shipping.
71. Advantages of Water Transport

Water transport is:

  • Energy efficient.
  • Suitable for bulky goods.
  • Relatively inexpensive for long-distance freight.
72. Limitations of Water Transport

Limitations include:

  • Slower speed.
  • Dependence on navigable channels and ports.
  • Seasonal water-level changes in rivers.
  • Need for transshipment to final destinations.
73. Inland Water Transport

Inland waterways include:

  • Rivers.
  • Canals.
  • Backwaters.
  • Lagoons.
74. Conditions for Navigable Rivers

A good inland waterway generally requires:

  • Adequate water depth.
  • Gentle gradient.
  • Stable channel.
  • Limited rapids and waterfalls.
  • Sufficient width.
75. Why Himalayan Plains Favour Waterways
  • Rivers have gentler gradients after entering plains.
  • Large rivers maintain substantial flow.
  • Dense population and agriculture create transport demand.
76. Problems of River Navigation

Problems include:

  • Siltation.
  • Shifting channels.
  • Seasonal flow.
  • Barrages.
  • Rapids.
  • Sandbars.
77. National Waterways — Concept
  • Important inland waterways can be designated as National Waterways.
  • They are developed for commercial navigation and transport.
78. National Waterway 1
  • National Waterway 1 follows the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hugli river system.
  • It connects the northern plains with the Kolkata-Haldia region.
📌Must-Memorise

NW-1 → Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hugli

79. National Waterway 2
  • National Waterway 2 follows the Brahmaputra River in Assam.
📌Must-Memorise

NW-2 → Brahmaputra

80. National Waterway 3
  • National Waterway 3 is associated with the West Coast Canal and connected waterways of Kerala.
📌Must-Memorise

NW-3 → Kerala West Coast Canal

81. Kerala Backwaters
  • Kerala has an extensive network of:
  • Lagoons.
  • Canals.
  • Backwaters.
  • These support inland navigation.
82. Vembanad Lake and Navigation
  • Vembanad Lake forms part of Kerala's important backwater transport system.
83. Coastal Shipping
  • Coastal shipping moves cargo between ports along India's coastline.
  • It can reduce pressure on roads and railways.
84. Ocean Transport
  • Ocean shipping carries most of India's international bulk trade by volume.
  • It is essential for:
  • Petroleum.
  • Coal.
  • Iron ore.
  • Containers.
  • Fertilisers.
85. Port
  • A port is a coastal or inland facility where ships load and unload:
  • Cargo.
  • Passengers.
86. Harbour
  • A harbour is a sheltered water area where ships can anchor safely.
  • A port includes commercial facilities, while a harbour mainly refers to the sheltered water body.
⚠️TNPSC Trap

Harbour ≠ Port

87. Natural Harbour
  • A natural harbour is protected by natural coastal features.
  • Mumbai is a classic Indian example.
📌Must-Memorise

Mumbai → Natural Harbour

88. Artificial Harbour
  • An artificial harbour is protected using man-made structures such as:
  • Breakwaters.
  • Sea walls.
  • Chennai is an important example.
📌Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Chennai → Artificial Harbour

89. Breakwater
  • A breakwater is a structure built offshore or near the coast to reduce wave energy and protect a harbour.
90. Major Ports of India — Geographic Awareness

Important ports include:

  • Deendayal/Kandla.
  • Mumbai.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru Port.
  • Mormugao.
  • New Mangalore.
  • Kochi.
  • Chennai.
  • Kamarajar.
  • V.O. Chidambaranar.
  • Visakhapatnam.
  • Paradip.
  • Kolkata-Haldia.
91. Deendayal Port
  • Deendayal Port, formerly Kandla, lies in Gujarat.
  • It is located in the Gulf of Kachchh region.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Kandla/Deendayal → Gujarat → Gulf of Kachchh

92. Mumbai Port
  • Mumbai Port lies on India's western coast.
  • It has an excellent natural harbour.
93. Jawaharlal Nehru Port
  • Jawaharlal Nehru Port lies near Mumbai.
  • It is a major container-handling port.
94. Mormugao Port
  • Mormugao Port lies in Goa.
  • It historically handled significant mineral exports, especially iron ore.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Mormugao → Goa

95. New Mangalore Port
  • New Mangalore Port lies on the Karnataka coast.
  • It serves the resource-rich hinterland of Karnataka.
96. Kochi Port
  • Kochi Port lies on Kerala's west coast.
  • Its location is associated with a natural backwater harbour system.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Kochi → Kerala

97. Chennai Port
  • Chennai Port lies on the Coromandel Coast.
  • It is an artificial harbour.
  • It is one of Tamil Nadu's major maritime gateways.
📌Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Chennai Port → Coromandel Coast → Artificial Harbour

98. Kamarajar Port
  • Kamarajar Port is located at Ennore north of Chennai.
  • It handles bulk cargo and other maritime traffic.
🔗Tamil Nadu Key Link

Kamarajar Port → Ennore

99. V.O. Chidambaranar Port
  • V.O. Chidambaranar Port lies at Thoothukudi.
  • It is one of southern Tamil Nadu's major ports.
📌Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

V.O.C. Port → Thoothukudi

100. Thoothukudi Harbour Geography
  • The Gulf of Mannar coast and proximity to major sea routes give Thoothukudi strategic maritime importance.
101. Visakhapatnam Port
  • Visakhapatnam lies on the Andhra Pradesh coast.
  • It has a naturally protected harbour setting.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

Visakhapatnam → Andhra Pradesh

102. Paradip Port
  • Paradip lies on the Odisha coast.
  • It serves the mineral-rich eastern hinterland.
103. Kolkata Port
  • Kolkata is a riverine port.
  • It lies on the Hugli River.
📌Must-Memorise

Kolkata → Riverine Port → Hugli

104. Haldia
  • Haldia lies downstream from Kolkata on the Hugli estuary.
  • It supplements the Kolkata port system.
105. Riverine Port
  • A riverine port lies along a navigable river rather than directly on the open coast.
  • Kolkata is India's classic example.
106. Hinterland
  • A port's hinterland is the inland region that supplies cargo to or receives cargo from the port.
📌Must-Memorise

Hinterland → Inland Area Served by a Port

107. Foreland
  • A port's foreland is the overseas region connected to it through shipping routes.
108. Port–Hinterland Relationship

Ports depend on:

  • Railways.
  • Highways.
  • Pipelines.
  • Industrial corridors.

to connect with their hinterlands.

109. Container Port
  • Container ports handle standardised containers.
  • Containers allow rapid transfer between ship, rail and truck.
110. Dry Port
  • A dry port is an inland freight terminal connected to seaports by road or rail.
  • It handles customs and container operations away from the coast.
📌TNPSC Advanced Fact

Dry Port → Inland Container Terminal

111. Inland Container Depot
  • Inland Container Depots facilitate:
  • Container handling.
  • Customs.
  • Rail/road transfer.
112. Airways — Basic Importance
  • Air transport is the fastest mode of transport.
  • It is especially useful for:
  • Long distances.
  • High-value goods.
  • Emergency transport.
  • Remote areas.
113. Advantages of Air Transport
  • Fastest transport.
  • Crosses difficult terrain easily.
  • Useful in mountains and islands.
  • Important for international travel.
114. Limitations of Air Transport
  • High cost.
  • Weather sensitivity.
  • Limited bulk-freight capacity.
  • High infrastructure requirements.
115. Airports and Metropolitan Cities

Major metropolitan air hubs include:

  • Delhi.
  • Mumbai.
  • Bengaluru.
  • Chennai.
  • Hyderabad.
  • Kolkata.
116. Chennai International Airport
  • Chennai International Airport is one of southern India's major aviation gateways.
  • It serves domestic and international traffic.
🔗Tamil Nadu Key Link

Chennai → Major South Indian Air Gateway

117. Tamil Nadu Airports

Important airports include:

  • Chennai.
  • Coimbatore.
  • Madurai.
  • Tiruchirappalli.
  • Thoothukudi.
  • Salem.
118. Tiruchirappalli Airport
  • Tiruchirappalli is an important aviation centre in central Tamil Nadu.
  • It serves domestic and international routes.
119. Coimbatore Airport
  • Coimbatore Airport serves western Tamil Nadu's major industrial region.
120. Madurai Airport
  • Madurai Airport serves southern Tamil Nadu and important tourism and pilgrimage centres.
121. Air Transport in Mountain Regions

Airways are particularly useful where:

  • Road construction is difficult.
  • Travel distances are long.
  • Natural disasters disrupt surface transport.
122. Air Transport in Islands

Air transport is vital for:

  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Lakshadweep.

because of geographical isolation.

123. Helicopter Transport

Helicopters are useful for:

  • Mountain rescue.
  • Defence.
  • Disaster relief.
  • Remote settlements.
  • Medical evacuation.
124. Pipeline Transport
  • Pipelines transport:
  • Petroleum.
  • Natural gas.
  • Refined products.
  • Water in some systems.
  • They provide continuous flow.
125. Advantages of Pipelines
  • Low operating cost after construction.
  • Reliable continuous transport.
  • Limited surface traffic congestion.
  • Useful across difficult terrain.
126. Limitations of Pipelines
  • High initial cost.
  • Leakage risk.
  • Limited mainly to fluids and gases.
  • Route security and maintenance are essential.
127. Petroleum Pipelines

Petroleum pipelines can carry:

  • Crude oil from fields to refineries.
  • Refined products from refineries to markets.
128. Natural Gas Pipelines
  • Gas pipelines connect:
  • Gas fields.
  • LNG terminals.
  • Fertiliser plants.
  • Power stations.
  • Cities.
129. Pipeline and Energy Geography

Pipelines reduce dependence on tanker trucks and rail wagons for continuous fuel transport.

130. Communication — Importance

Communication facilitates:

  • Governance.
  • Business.
  • Education.
  • Disaster warnings.
  • Banking.
  • Health services.
  • Social interaction.
131. Postal Communication
  • Postal services provide:
  • Letters.
  • Parcels.
  • Financial and other services.
  • They remain important in rural areas.
132. Telecommunication

Telecommunication includes:

  • Landline telephone.
  • Mobile telephone.
  • Internet.
  • Satellite links.
  • Fibre-optic systems.
133. Mobile Communication
  • Mobile networks transmit voice and data using radio waves through cellular networks.
  • Cellular coverage is divided into geographic cells.
134. Base Station
  • A base station connects mobile devices to the telecommunications network.
135. Internet
  • The internet is a global network of interconnected computer networks.
  • It supports:
  • Communication.
  • Commerce.
  • Education.
  • Digital services.
136. Broadband
  • Broadband refers to high-capacity internet connectivity.
  • It can be delivered through:
  • Fibre.
  • Cable.
  • Mobile networks.
  • Satellite.
137. Optical Fibre
  • Optical-fibre cables transmit information as pulses of light.
  • They offer:
  • Very high data capacity.
  • Low signal loss.
  • High transmission speed.
📌Must-Memorise

Optical Fibre → Data Through Light

138. Fibre-Optic Communication
  • Fibre networks form the backbone of modern telecommunications.
  • They connect:
  • Cities.
  • Data centres.
  • Mobile towers.
  • International networks.
139. Submarine Cable
  • Submarine cables are fibre-optic cables laid on the ocean floor.
  • They carry a large share of international internet traffic.
🔗TNPSC Key Link

International Internet → Mainly Submarine Fibre Cables

140. Satellite Communication

Satellites support:

  • Television.
  • Telephone.
  • Internet.
  • Navigation.
  • Weather forecasting.
  • Disaster communication.
141. Geostationary Satellite
  • A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator.
  • It appears fixed over one point on Earth.
  • It is useful for communication and weather observation.
142. Satellite Communication Advantage

Satellites are particularly useful for:

  • Islands.
  • Mountains.
  • Ships.
  • Remote areas.
143. Radio Communication
  • Radio transmits information using electromagnetic waves.
  • It can cover wide areas with relatively simple receiving equipment.
144. Television Communication
  • Television uses terrestrial, cable, satellite and internet-based transmission systems.
145. Mass Communication

Mass communication reaches large audiences.

Examples include:

  • Newspapers.
  • Radio.
  • Television.
  • Internet platforms.
146. Communication and Disaster Management

Communication networks are essential for:

  • Cyclone warnings.
  • Flood alerts.
  • Tsunami warnings.
  • Evacuation instructions.
  • Emergency coordination.
147. Early Warning System
  • An early warning system combines:
  • Hazard detection.
  • Forecasting.
  • Communication.
  • Community response.
148. Communication and Agriculture

Farmers can receive:

  • Weather forecasts.
  • Market prices.
  • Pest alerts.
  • Irrigation advice.
  • Crop recommendations.
149. Communication and Markets

Digital communication enables:

  • Price discovery.
  • Online trade.
  • Banking.
  • Logistics coordination.
150. Transport and Communication Integration

Modern logistics depends on both:

  • Physical movement of goods.
  • Rapid movement of information.
151. Logistics
  • Logistics is the planning and management of movement and storage of goods.
  • It includes:
  • Transport.
  • Warehousing.
  • Inventory.
  • Information flow.
152. Supply Chain
  • A supply chain connects:
  • Producers.
  • Processors.
  • Warehouses.
  • Transporters.
  • Retailers.
  • Consumers.
153. Logistics Hub
  • A logistics hub is a location where goods are:
  • Stored.
  • Sorted.
  • Transferred.
  • Distributed.
  • Good road, rail and port connectivity is essential.
154. Industrial Corridor
  • An industrial corridor combines:
  • Transport infrastructure.
  • Industrial zones.
  • Urban centres.
  • Logistics facilities.
  • It can stimulate regional development.
155. Transport Corridor
  • A transport corridor is a concentrated route linking major economic centres.
  • It may contain highways, railways and pipelines.
156. Transport Node
  • A transport node is an important junction where routes meet.
  • Major cities often develop as transport nodes.
157. Chennai as a Transport Node

Chennai combines:

  • National highways.
  • Rail terminals.
  • Metro rail.
  • Seaport.
  • Airport.
  • Industrial corridors.
🔗Tamil Nadu Key Link

Chennai → Major Multimodal Transport Hub

158. Chennai Metropolitan Transport

Important modes include:

  • Suburban railway.
  • Metro rail.
  • Buses.
  • Roads.

  • What is broadband? → High-capacity internet connectivity.
